about: The vetted list of the presence wording check (test/presence-wording.test.ts, P4). Every sentence in the docs, the sources' comments and messages, the scripts and the printed output that mentions presence, the UP flag, a touch of a key, hardware, a security key or a YubiKey must carry the limit wording (test/helpers/wording.ts, LIMIT_WORDING) or appear here, vetted by a person as stating no claim of hardware-verified presence or of a person proven present. Entries are matched after normalisation (whitespace, fingerprints, long hex, numbers). Add a sentence only after reading it in place; a claim the deny-list catches fails whatever is listed here.

reasonsExplained.history: History: the draft design record, the design stages and earlier rounds' build notes record what was planned, built, run and found then; they are not rewritten, and the current limit is stated where the level is defined (security model, refined §U9)
reasonsExplained.names: Names the level, the unit, a requirement, a file or a test, or shows the configuration and the level enum: no statement about people or hardware
reasonsExplained.mechanism: Describes the flag, the key types or the per-verdict signature mechanism (what is signed, what is checked, what one touch signs): no statement that a person or hardware was verified; the limit is stated in the same section
reasonsExplained.ssh-keygen: Describes OpenSSH's own behaviour (ssh-keygen, git verify-commit, the sk-dummy middleware, FIDO flag bits)
reasonsExplained.output: A message pr-rla prints while signing or checking: it describes the key, its flag and the level given, never a person
reasonsExplained.notes: This round's build notes (P4): the findings, the tests that cover them and what was measured; the limit itself is stated in the security model and printed on every certificate

ssh-keygen -Y verify does not enforce the presence flag (settles the design's open item).

No option requires the flag: -Y verify takes -O hashalg, print-pubkey and verify-time only, and the allowed-signers options are cert-authority, namespaces, valid-after and valid-before; in the source, sig_verify only logs the flags at debug2. no-touch-required and verify-required exist only as certificate and key-generation options in ssh-keygen, and as authorized_keys options for sshd. git verify-commit inherits this: the fixture's UP-clear commits (draws #4 and #5) verify with exit 0.
So a team verifying with git or ssh-keygen alone would accept a touch-less signature; pr-rla checks the flag itself.

An empty blame.ignoreRevsFile does not clear a configured ignore list. git inserts the configured files into a sorted list, so "" sorts first and clears nothing; a verifier whose git configuration names an ignore-revs file would have had lines moved to other commits. --no-ignore-revs-file clears it, and the ledger passes it (git-file-presence.test.ts › an ignore-revs list…).

This round fixes every finding on the same branch, bolt/u9-presence-verdicts, in the same worktree, and replaces the verdict mechanism on the coordinator's decision.

A line's provenance was its commit's signature, so one signing touch covered every line in the commit: an assistant appends 35 verdicts naming the reviewer, the reviewer's next git commit -S -a makes all 35 presence (finding 4).

Finding a line's commit needs git blame, which a verifier's checkout can steer: in a --depth 1 clone (a CI checkout's default) every line is attributed to the boundary commit and takes its signer's level (finding 1, reproduced: 7/7 PASS, CERTIFIED, presence (35)); grafts, a hand-written .git/shallow, a rename hidden behind a merge (finding 2, reproduced on a full clone), textconv and commit-graph files steer it too (finding 5).
So one touch signs exactly one verdict, for one draw of one registration (findings 4 and 8 closed by construction).

pr-rla record <draw> pass|fail --sign <key> writes the bytes to a temporary file, runs ssh-keygen -Y sign -n pr-rla-verdict@v1 -f <key> <file> (a security key asks for its touch), checks the signature as verify will, and appends the line.
A reviewer signs each verdict (one touch each with a security key) instead of each commit; git commit -S is no longer needed.

mechanism: Verdict provenance: self-asserted; with the reviewers' SSH keys registered and each verdict signed on its own (pr-rla record --sign), account, or presence with a FIDO security key and the user-presence flag set ([signed verdicts](#signed-verdicts-git-file), below).
So one signature, which with a security key is one touch, is one verdict on one draw of one frozen audit, and it cannot be made before the seed is public.
It means the verdict's own signature carries the user-presence flag from a registered security key.

Verification (src/core/presence, pure) rebuilds the bytes from the line's fields and the audit being verified: the registration's digest, and the manifest digest and beacon round and randomness verify has already checked (status and record read them from manifest.json and draws.json).
One touch signs exactly one verdict, for one draw of one registration.

the issue ledgers (the label event's actor and created_at); a git-file line signed by the registered software SSH key of the reviewer it names, or by their registered security key with the user-presence flag clear
as account, and the signature carries the FIDO user-presence (UP) flag from the reviewer's registered security key
a git-file line signed by the registered sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com or sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com key of the reviewer it names, UP set

With a security key, one touch signs exactly one verdict: an assistant that appends lines in the reviewer's shell cannot have them all vouched for by the next touch, a line cannot move to another draw or another audit, and rebasing, cherry-picking or amending other people's commits signs nothing that counts.

Under a registration that registers keys and sets require_signed or a minimum above self-asserted, a line without a valid signature by its reviewer's registered key is ineligible: it is ignored, with its reason, as a bot's label is, and the first eligible signed verdict for the change counts. status, check 7 and record apply the same rule (countedVerdicts in src/core/presence/provenance.ts), so unsigned lines an assistant appended first can neither stand in for the reviewer's signed verdict nor keep record --sign from recording it.

register refuses rules no verdict could meet (account with git-file and no keys, presence with no registered security key, require_signed with no keys or another ledger, keys with any ledger but git-file), and warns when keys are registered but neither require_signed nor a minimum above self-asserted is set, since unsigned verdicts would then still count.
for a security key, reads the UP flag (bit 0x01) itself.

A ledger cannot raise a verdict above what it can attest: presence comes only from this check of a git-file line, the issue ledgers top out at account (a label event carries no presence evidence), and an external ledger is never counted above account.
Check 7 WARNs on an unreadable, invalid or foreign signature, an unlisted key, a signer who is not the reviewer the line names, and a security key whose signature counter goes down.

A touch request from a key you use only for verdicts at least tells you that some verdict is being signed, though not which one (next point); one from the key that also signs your commits and SSH logins is easy to grant without looking.
A touch is presence for one signature, not a review.
The authenticator does not show what it signs, so a reviewer could be talked into touching for a verdict they did not make.
True for the FIDO security-key types.
Security keys: the FIDO application string (usually ssh:).
presence means pr-rla verified a FIDO user-presence flag in the signature.

Lowers any verdict claiming more than the ledger can attest. presence is granted only by pr-rla's own check of a verdict's signature (with the git-file ledger); issue-tracker ledgers top out at account, because a label event carries no presence evidence.

The default minimum is the ledger's own level (account with an issue ledger, self-asserted with git-file); git-file reaches account only with registered SSH keys and presence only with a registered security key; keys and require_signed count only with the built-in git-file.

ssh-keygen: The reviewer signs as they record: pr-rla record 7 pass --sign ~/keys/verdicts_sk. pr-rla writes the bytes to a temporary file, runs ssh-keygen -Y sign -n pr-rla-verdict@v1 -f <key> <file> (a security key asks for its touch), checks the signature as verify will, and appends the line; the reviewer is the key's registered principal.

(A value holding " or \ would need JSON escaping in the line; change ids and principals hold neither.) verify checks each line's SSHSIG in TypeScript, without ssh-keygen: the key must be registered, the line's reviewer must be that key's principal exactly, the signature must be for this registration, manifest and seed (verify rebuilds the bytes from what it has verified, and refuses pr-rla-verdict/v1 signatures, which named neither), and for a security key (sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com, sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com) the user-presence flag must be set for presence.
ssh-keygen -Y verify and git verify-commit do not enforce the presence flag.

OpenSSH 10.3p1 accepts a security-key signature whose UP flag is clear, and neither -Y verify nor the allowed-signers format has an option that requires it (checked 2026-11-04; test/presence-oracle.test.ts). pr-rla checks the flag itself; verifying with ssh-keygen alone would accept a touch-less signature. ssh-keygen also accepts things pr-rla refuses on purpose: a small-order Ed25519 key whose one "signature" verifies every message, RSA keys of 1024 to 2047 bits, a non-empty reserved field, and WebAuthn signatures.
sign this verdict with your registered SSH key (ssh-keygen -Y sign; a security key asks for a touch)
FIDO security-key types (OpenSSH PROTOCOL.u2f): their signatures carry a flags byte and a counter.

For FIDO security keys it rebuilds what the authenticator signed (OpenSSH PROTOCOL.u2f): SHA256(application) ‖ flags ‖ counter ‖ SHA256(signed data), and returns the flags byte, so the caller can check the user-presence (UP) flag itself: OpenSSH's ssh-keygen -Y verify accepts a signature whether or not UP is set.

Where pr-rla is deliberately stricter than ssh-keygen (test/presence-oracle.test.ts shows each): a non-empty reserved field, RSA keys under 2048 bits or with a public exponent of 1 or an even one, small-order Ed25519 keys, security keys whose application does not start with ssh:, and webauthn-sk-* signatures are refused.
FIDO flags (sk-api.h): bit 0 user present (UP), bit 2 user verified (UV).
A security key's counter going down, in ledger order, is a WARN, never a FAIL: authenticators differ (some always report 0, OpenSSH's test middleware a constant).
ssh-keygen's own messages (the touch request among them) reach the reviewer as they come.
